subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 11! In this unit you will explore the world of three-dimensional shapes – the solid objects that fill the space all around you. Every box of dates in the Hargeisa market, every water tank on a rooftop in Mogadishu, every football kicked in the street, and every brick in the walls of the masjid is a 3D shape. Unlike the flat 2D shapes you have studied before, 3D shapes have length, width and height. They take up real space, they hold volume, and they have surfaces you could paint or wrap.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Name and describe the common 3D shapes and their properties.
Count the faces, edges and vertices of a solid accurately.
Recognise how simple shapes combine to form compound 3D shapes.
Draw and identify nets for cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids.
Calculate the surface area of cubes and cuboids from their nets or formulas.
Calculate the volume of cubes and cuboids using V = length × width × height.
Solve real-world problems involving surface area and volume.

concepts.title: What Makes a Shape 3D?
concepts.explanation:
A three-dimensional (3D) shape has three measurements: length, width and height. This is what separates it from a flat 2D shape like a square or a circle, which has only length and width. Because a 3D shape has that third measurement, it takes up space in the real world and it has an inside as well as an outside. A drawing of a square on paper is 2D; a real dice you can pick up and turn over is 3D.

Every solid shape (called a polyhedron when all its faces are flat) can be described using three key features. Learn these three words carefully, because you will use them constantly:

Faces – the flat surfaces that make up the shape. Each face is itself a 2D shape, such as a square or a triangle.

Edges – the straight lines where two faces meet. Run your finger along the join between two faces and you are tracing an edge.

Vertices – the corner points where edges meet. One corner is a vertex; several are vertices.

Let us count these for a cube, using a sugar cube or a dice as a model. A cube has 6 faces, and every one is an identical square. It has 12 edges, all exactly the same length. And it has 8 vertices, one at each corner. Hold a dice and check: the six numbered faces are the faces, the sharp lines between them are the edges, and the eight pointed corners are the vertices. Counting from a real object is always easier than counting from a flat picture, so pick up an object whenever you can.

There is a beautiful pattern connecting these three numbers, discovered by the mathematician Leonhard Euler. For any solid with flat faces (a polyhedron), vertices − edges + faces = 2. Written shorter, V − E + F = 2. Test it on the cube: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. It works! Test it on a square-based pyramid: it has 5 vertices, 8 edges and 5 faces, so 5 − 8 + 5 = 2. This rule is a wonderful way to check that you have counted correctly. If your three numbers do not give 2, you have miscounted something.
concepts.example: One warning that catches many learners: curved solids like spheres, cylinders and cones are not polyhedra, so Euler's rule does not apply to them, and their curved surfaces are not really 'faces' in the strict sense. A cylinder is often said to have '2 flat circular faces and 1 curved surface', but the curved surface is not a flat face and a cylinder has no true vertices. Be careful and precise when a shape has curves.

concepts.title: The Common 3D Shapes
concepts.explanation: Let us meet the family of solids you need to know well. For each one, picture a real object from around your home or town, and learn its properties. A table like this is worth reading several times until the numbers become automatic. The cube and the cuboid are the two shapes you will work with most in this unit. They are closely related: both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. The difference is that a cube's faces are all identical squares, while a cuboid (also called a rectangular prism) has rectangular faces, and opposite faces are equal but not all six are identical.
concepts.example: A prism is any solid that has the same cross-section all the way along its length. If you were to slice a triangular prism straight across at any point, you would always see the same triangle. A cuboid is really a rectangular prism, because slicing it gives the same rectangle everywhere. This idea of a constant cross-section is important later when you calculate volume, because volume of a prism is simply the area of the cross-section multiplied by the length.

concepts.title: Compound 3D Shapes
concepts.explanation:
Most real objects are not single simple solids – they are compound shapes made by joining two or more basic solids together. Learning to break a complicated object into simple pieces is one of the most powerful skills in geometry, because once you can see the pieces, you can measure each one and add the results.

Think about a typical house. The main building is a cuboid, and the roof on top is a triangular prism. Put them together and you have described the whole house with just two familiar shapes. A tall tower on a mosque or a fort might be a cylinder with a cone on top for its roof. A rocket is a cylinder for its body, a cone for its nose, and smaller cylinders for its boosters. Once you start looking, you will see compound shapes everywhere.

To describe a compound shape clearly, use a simple four-step method:

Identify the main shape – the largest solid that forms the body of the object.

Identify the added shapes – the smaller solids attached to or sitting on the main shape.

Describe the relationships – say how the pieces are joined (on top of, attached to the side, and so on).

Use precise mathematical language – name each piece exactly, for example 'a triangular prism resting on a cuboid'.
concepts.example: For example, Khadija might describe the water tower at Nuur Academy like this: 'This structure is made of a tall cylinder for the tank, sitting on four thin cuboids that act as legs, with a shallow cone as the lid on top.' That single sentence captures the whole object in the language of solids. When you meet a surface-area or volume problem about a compound shape, this same skill lets you measure each simple piece and then combine the pieces – adding for surfaces that show, and being careful about surfaces that become hidden where two shapes join.

concepts.title: Nets of 3D Shapes
concepts.explanation:
A net is a flat, 2D pattern that folds up to make a 3D shape. If you took a cardboard box, carefully cut along some of its edges, and unfolded it until it lay flat on the table, the flat pattern you would see is the net of that box. Nets are the bridge between the 2D world of paper and the 3D world of solids, and they matter enormously in real life: every cereal box, milk carton and shipping crate begins life as a flat net that a machine folds and glues into shape.

Let us look at the nets of the shapes you know:

Cube net – six squares joined edge to edge. The most familiar arrangement is a cross or plus shape: a vertical line of four squares with one square sticking out on each side of the second square. Amazingly, there are 11 different nets that all fold into a cube.

Cuboid net – six rectangles in three matching pairs. A common layout is a strip of four rectangles going around the sides, with the top and bottom rectangles attached above and below.

Triangular prism net – two triangles (the ends) and three rectangles (the sides) that wrap around them.

Square pyramid net – one square in the centre with four triangles, one attached to each side of the square, that fold up to meet at the apex.

Cylinder net – two circles (the ends) and one rectangle whose length equals the distance around the circle (its circumference).
concepts.example: Being able to picture a net folding up, and a solid unfolding into a net, is a skill of mental visualisation. Practise it by taking a real box apart and by folding paper nets you draw yourself. The reward is huge: once you can see a shape as its net, calculating its surface area becomes simple, because the net lays out every single face flat where you can measure it.

concepts.title: Surface Area
concepts.explanation:
Surface area is the total area of all the faces of a 3D shape added together. It tells you how much material you would need to cover the outside of an object completely – how much paint to coat a wall, how much card to make a box, or how much wrapping paper to cover a gift. Surface area is measured in square units, such as square centimetres (cm²) or square metres (m²), because it is an area.

The easiest and safest way to find surface area is to think about the net. Because the net shows every face flat, you simply work out the area of each face and add them all up. Nothing is hidden and nothing is counted twice. Let us do this carefully for a cube and a cuboid.

A cube has 6 identical square faces. If each edge is 4 cm, then each square face has area 4 × 4 = 16 cm². There are 6 of them, so the total surface area is 6 × 16 = 96 cm². This gives us a neat formula: Surface area of a cube = 6 × (edge length)², often written 6 × edge². For a cube with edge 10 cm, the surface area is 6 × 10² = 6 × 100 = 600 cm².

A cuboid has three pairs of matching rectangular faces. Take a cuboid measuring 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. Its three different faces are: the 6 × 4 face (area 24 cm²), the 6 × 3 face (area 18 cm²), and the 4 × 3 face (area 12 cm²). Each of these appears twice, so the surface area is 2(24) + 2(18) + 2(12) = 48 + 36 + 24 = 108 cm².

This leads to the standard cuboid formula. If the length is l, the width is w and the height is h, then the surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh). Check it on our example: 2(6×4 + 6×3 + 4×3) = 2(24 + 18 + 12) = 2(54) = 108 cm². The formula and the net method always agree, which is why you can use one to check the other. When a problem asks for only some of the faces – for example, painting the four walls and ceiling of a room but not the floor – you simply add the areas of the faces you need and leave out the rest.
concepts.example: A common real-world example is painting a room. Suppose a store room is 4 m long, 3 m wide and 2.5 m high, and you must paint the four walls and the ceiling but not the floor. The ceiling is 4 × 3 = 12 m². Two walls are 4 × 2.5 = 10 m² each, and the other two walls are 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 m² each. Adding these gives 12 + 10 + 10 + 7.5 + 7.5 = 47 m² of surface to paint. Working face by face, exactly as the net suggests, stops you from forgetting a wall or including the floor by mistake.

concepts.title: Volume of Cubes and Cuboids
concepts.explanation:
Volume is the amount of space inside a 3D shape – how much it can hold. While surface area covers the outside, volume fills the inside. Volume is measured in cubic units, such as cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³), because it fills three dimensions at once. One cubic centimetre is the space taken up by a tiny cube measuring 1 cm along every edge.

Picture filling a cuboid box with little 1 cm cubes. Suppose the box is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. Along the bottom you could fit 5 × 3 = 15 cubes in a single layer. The box is 2 layers high, so altogether it holds 15 × 2 = 30 little cubes. Each cube is 1 cm³, so the volume is 30 cm³. This is exactly what the formula says: Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height, written V = l × w × h. For our box, V = 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³.

A cube is just a cuboid with all three measurements equal, so its volume formula is even simpler: Volume of a cube = edge × edge × edge = edge³. A storage cube with 4 cm edges has volume 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³. Notice the difference between surface area and volume for the very same cube: its surface area is 6 × 4² = 96 cm² (square units), while its volume is 4³ = 64 cm³ (cubic units). Keeping these two ideas separate – outside covering versus inside space, square units versus cubic units – is one of the most important things you will learn this unit.
concepts.example: Volume matters constantly in real life. When Yusuf works out how many boxes of dates will fit in the back of a lorry, he is comparing volumes. When Farah fills a water tank, the volume tells her how many litres it holds (and helpfully, 1000 cm³ equals exactly 1 litre). When a builder orders concrete for a foundation, he multiplies length by width by depth to know how many cubic metres to buy. Let us work one example. A water tank shaped like a cuboid is 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1 m deep. Its volume is 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 m³, which is 3000 litres of water. Always multiply all three measurements, and always give the answer in cubic units.

methods.title: How to find the surface area of a cuboid
methods.example: A cereal box measures 22 cm long, 8 cm wide and 30 cm high. How much cardboard is needed to cover its surface completely?
steps: Identify the three different faces: l×w, l×h and w×h.
Work out the area of each of the three faces.
Each face appears twice, so add them and double: 2(lw + lh + wh).
Write the answer in square units (cm² or m²).

methods.title: How to find the volume of a cuboid
methods.example: A fish tank is 50 cm long, 25 cm wide and 30 cm high. What is its volume?
steps: Write down the length, width and height in the same units.
Multiply length × width to find the area of the base.
Multiply that result by the height.
Write the answer in cubic units (cm³ or m³).

methods.title: How to describe a compound shape
methods.example: A grain silo is made from a cylinder body with a cone-shaped top. How would you describe this compound shape?
steps: Find the main (largest) solid.
Find the smaller solids attached to it.
Describe how they are joined (on top, beside, inside).

methods.title: Surface area of a cuboid
methods.example: A shoe box measures 20 cm long, 15 cm wide and 10 cm high. How much wrapping paper is needed to cover it exactly?
steps: Use 2(lw + lh + wh).
So 1300 cm² of paper covers the box with none spare.

methods.title: Volume of a cuboid
methods.example: A crate for carrying mangoes is 60 cm long, 40 cm wide and 30 cm high. What is its volume?
steps: Volume = length × width × height = 60 × 40 × 30.
Because 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, the crate holds 72 litres of space.

methods.title: Volume of a cube
methods.example: A storage cube has edges of 5 cm. Find its volume, and also its surface area, and explain why the units differ.
steps: Volume = edge³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³ (cubic units, because it fills space).
Surface area = 6 × edge² = 6 × 25 = 150 cm² (square units, because it covers the outside).
Volume uses cubic units and surface area uses square units — always keep them separate.

workedExamples.title: Count faces, edges and vertices
workedExamples.prompt: A triangular prism is used as a tent shape. How many faces, edges and vertices does it have, and does it satisfy Euler's rule?
workedExamples.solution: A triangular prism has 2 triangular faces plus 3 rectangular faces, giving 5 faces. It has 9 edges (3 around each triangle makes 6, plus 3 joining them). It has 6 vertices (3 at each triangular end). Check Euler: V − E + F = 6 − 9 + 5 = 2. Correct, so our counting is right.

workedExamples.title: Identify a net
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan has a flat pattern made of 1 square and 4 identical triangles, one triangle joined to each side of the square. What solid does it fold into?
workedExamples.solution: The square becomes the base and the four triangles fold up to meet at a single point, so this is the net of a square-based pyramid. Its 4 triangular faces meet at one apex above the square base.

workedExamples.title: Surface area of a cube
workedExamples.prompt: A company makes cubic gift boxes with edges of 10 cm. How much card is needed for the surface of one box?
workedExamples.solution: Each square face is 10 × 10 = 100 cm². A cube has 6 faces, so the surface area is 6 × 100 = 600 cm². Using the formula 6 × edge² gives the same result: 6 × 10² = 600 cm².

workedExamples.title: Surface area of a cuboid
workedExamples.prompt: A shoe box measures 20 cm long, 15 cm wide and 10 cm high. How much wrapping paper is needed to cover it exactly?
workedExamples.solution: Use 2(lw + lh + wh). That is 2(20×15 + 20×10 + 15×10) = 2(300 + 200 + 150) = 2(650) = 1300 cm². So 1300 cm² of paper covers the box with none spare.

workedExamples.title: Volume of a cuboid
workedExamples.prompt: A crate for carrying mangoes is 60 cm long, 40 cm wide and 30 cm high. What is its volume?
workedExamples.solution: Volume = length × width × height = 60 × 40 × 30. First 60 × 40 = 2400, then 2400 × 30 = 72 000 cm³. Because 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, the crate holds 72 litres of space.

workedExamples.title: Volume of a cube
workedExamples.prompt: A storage cube has edges of 5 cm. Find its volume, and also its surface area, and explain why the units differ.
workedExamples.solution: Volume = edge³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³ (cubic units, because it fills space). Surface area = 6 × edge² = 6 × 25 = 150 cm² (square units, because it covers the outside). Volume uses cubic units and surface area uses square units — always keep them separate.

workedExamples.title: Only some faces
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular swimming pool is 25 m long, 10 m wide and 2 m deep. Tiles are needed for the bottom and the four sides, but not the top (the water surface). What area must be tiled?
workedExamples.solution: Bottom = 25 × 10 = 250 m². The two long sides are 25 × 2 = 50 m² each, giving 100 m². The two short sides are 10 × 2 = 20 m² each, giving 40 m². Total = 250 + 100 + 40 = 390 m². We left out the top face because it is open water.

workedExamples.title: A painted-cube puzzle
workedExamples.prompt: A 3 × 3 × 3 cube (27 small cubes) is painted red on the outside, then split apart. How many small cubes have exactly 2 red faces?
workedExamples.solution: Cubes with exactly 2 red faces sit along the edges of the big cube but are not corners. Each of the 12 edges of a cube has one such middle cube, so there are 12 small cubes with exactly 2 red faces. (For the record: 8 corners have 3 faces, 6 face-centres have 1 face, and 1 hidden centre has 0 — and 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27.)

activities.title: 3D Shape Detective
activities.materials: your eyes, a notebook, and objects around your home.
steps: Hunt for 5 cubes or cuboids (boxes, books, tins of matches), 3 cylinders (tins, tubes), and 2 spheres (a ball, an orange).
For each object, record how many faces, edges and vertices it has.
Note what 2D shapes make up its faces (squares, rectangles, circles).
Choose one object and check its counts with Euler's rule: V − E + F = 2.
Keep your notebook – it becomes a personal catalogue of the solids around you.

activities.title: Net Construction Workshop
activities.materials: an empty cardboard box (a cereal or tea box is ideal), scissors, a ruler.
steps: Carefully cut along some edges of the box and unfold it until it lies flat.
You are now looking at the box's net. Count the rectangles – there should be 6, in 3 matching pairs.
Measure each rectangle and work out the surface area of the whole box.
Fold it back up to check your net really does make the box, then try drawing a different net for the same box.

activities.title: Surface Area vs Volume Laboratory
activities.materials: a small box or tin, a ruler, paper for calculations.
steps: Measure the length, width and height of your box in centimetres.
Calculate its surface area using 2(lw + lh + wh) – this is how much paper would cover it.
Calculate its volume using length × width × height – this is how much it holds.
Write both answers with their units and explain to a family member, or your AI tutor if none are available, why one is in cm² and the other in cm³.

activities.title: Build a Cube from Sugar Cubes
activities.materials: small identical cubes (sugar cubes, dice, or paper cubes you make).
steps: Build a 2 × 2 × 2 cube. How many small cubes did you use? (Answer: 8.)
Build a 3 × 3 × 3 cube. How many small cubes now? (Answer: 27.) Notice the pattern: edge³.
Imagine painting the outside of your 3 × 3 × 3 cube. Predict how many small cubes would have 3, 2, 1 and 0 painted faces.
Take the cube apart to check your prediction (8 corners, 12 edges, 6 centres, 1 middle).

activities.title: Packaging Design Challenge (Family Task)
activities.materials: card, scissors, tape, a ruler, and a small object to package (a bar of soap works well).
steps: Measure the object and design a cuboid box that will hold it snugly.
Draw the net of your box on card, including small flaps for gluing.
Cut, fold and tape your box together, then check the object fits.
Calculate the surface area (card used) and volume (space inside). Which box design uses the least card? Discuss with your family, or your AI tutor if no one is available.

activities.title: 3D Shapes in Architecture Investigation
activities.materials: a walk around your town, a notebook, or pictures of famous buildings.
steps: Look at buildings, water towers, and the masjid. Sketch each one.
Break every structure into simple solids: cuboids for walls, cylinders for towers, cones or pyramids for roofs.
Write a sentence describing each building as a compound shape, using precise shape names.
Explain why an architect might choose each shape – strength, space, or beauty.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand the difference between surface area and volume best? What was the trickiest part? Which 3D shape do you now notice most often around you? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Euler's Rule for Polyhedra
rules.text: There is a beautiful pattern connecting these three numbers, discovered by the mathematician Leonhard Euler. For any solid with flat faces (a polyhedron), vertices − edges + faces = 2. Written shorter, V − E + F = 2. Test it on the cube: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. It works! Test it on a square-based pyramid: it has 5 vertices, 8 edges and 5 faces, so 5 − 8 + 5 = 2. This rule is a wonderful way to check that you have counted correctly. If your three numbers do not give 2, you have miscounted something.

rules.title: Curved Solids and Euler's Rule
rules.text: One warning that catches many learners: curved solids like spheres, cylinders and cones are not polyhedra, so Euler's rule does not apply to them, and their curved surfaces are not really 'faces' in the strict sense. A cylinder is often said to have '2 flat circular faces and 1 curved surface', but the curved surface is not a flat face and a cylinder has no true vertices. Be careful and precise when a shape has curves.

rules.title: 🤖 Ask Your AI Tutor
rules.text: 🤖 Ask Your AI Tutor Ask your AI tutor to name a 3D shape and quiz you on its faces, edges and vertices. Say: Give me three solids and let me check each one with Euler's rule V minus E plus F equals 2.

rules.title: Surface Area Formula for a Cuboid
rules.text: To find the surface area of a cuboid, use the formula 2(lw + lh + wh), where l, w and h are its length, width and height. This works because a cuboid has three pairs of identical rectangular faces.

rules.title: Edges vs Vertices
rules.text: Mixing up edges and vertices. An edge is a line; a vertex is a corner point. Count them separately and check with Euler's rule V − E + F = 2.

rules.title: Quick Check: Euler's Rule
rules.text: Check face-edge-vertex counts with Euler's rule V − E + F = 2 for any polyhedron.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Two cuboids each have a volume of 36 cm³. Cuboid A is 6 × 3 × 2 and Cuboid B is 9 × 4 × 1. Work out both surface areas and say which is larger.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A: 2(6×3 + 6×2 + 3×2) = 2(18+12+6) = 72 cm²; B: 2(9×4 + 9×1 + 4×1) = 2(36+9+4) = 98 cm². Cuboid B has the larger surface area even though both hold 36 cm³ – the flatter, longer box needs more covering.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Surface Area.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Surface area is the total area of all the faces of a 3D shape added together. It tells you how much material you would need to cover the outside of an object completely – how much paint to coat a wall, how much card to make a box, or how much wrapping paper to cover a gift. Surface area is measured in square units, such as square centimetres (cm²) or square metres (m²), because it is an area.

The easiest and safest way to find surface area is to think about the net. Because the net shows every face flat, you simply work out the area of each face and add them all up. Nothing is hidden and nothing is counted twice. Let us do this carefully for a cube and a cuboid.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Volume of Cubes and Cuboids.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Volume is the amount of space inside a 3D shape – how much it can hold. While surface area covers the outside, volume fills the inside. Volume is measured in cubic units, such as cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³), because it fills three dimensions at once. One cubic centimetre is the space taken up by a tiny cube measuring 1 cm along every edge.

Picture filling a cuboid box with little 1 cm cubes. Suppose the box is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. Along the bottom you could fit 5 × 3 = 15 cubes in a single layer. The box is 2 layers high, so altogether it holds 15 × 2 = 30 little cubes. Each cube is 1 cm³, so the volume is 30 cm³. This is exactly what the formula says: Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height, written V = l × w × h. For our box, V = 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³.
